exp: (a) i-1, physically located in us-east-1a, becomes unreachable and effectively fails along with the rest of that AZ's power and network infrastructure. (b) i-2 and i-3, in us-east-1b and us-east-1c, are unaffected, since they run on independent power, cooling, and network infrastructure; the ALB's health checks detect that i-1 has stopped responding, mark it unhealthy, and stop routing new traffic to it, continuing to serve all traffic from i-2 and i-3. (c) The S3 data in the app-data bucket remains fully available and intact, because S3 (unlike an EC2 instance, which is launched into and stays tied to one specific AZ) stores object data redundantly across multiple AZs within the Region as an intrinsic part of how the service itself works, not as something the customer had to configure.
expl: This scenario isolates the difference between AZ-pinned resources and Region-scoped, AWS-managed redundancy. EC2 instances are provisioned into a specific subnet, and a subnet lives in exactly one AZ -- so i-1 genuinely goes down with its AZ, with no automatic recovery of that specific instance. The ALB's job is precisely to paper over exactly this kind of partial failure: its health checks are running continuously in the background regardless of whether anything has gone wrong, so the moment i-1 stops responding, it's excluded from the routing pool within a couple of failed health-check intervals, and clients simply keep getting served -- now entirely by the two surviving AZs, at reduced total capacity rather than zero capacity. S3 sits in a different category entirely: you never chose an AZ when you created the bucket or wrote an object, because S3's durability design already spreads object data across multiple AZs within the Region behind the scenes as part of the base service -- this is exactly the kind of built-in resilience that the earlier explanation about durability vs. AZ-pinned compute resources is pointing at.

The original `"Resource": "*"` is a wildcard that matches every resource ARN in existence, across every AWS service and every bucket in the account -- not just objects in one bucket. The fix scopes the Resource field to `arn:aws:s3:::reports-bucket/*`, an ARN pattern that only matches object keys within the reports-bucket bucket specifically. It's worth noting a companion mistake this same misunderstanding often produces: if the role also needed to call `s3:ListBucket` (to enumerate what's in the bucket, as opposed to reading a specific known object), that action applies to the bucket's own ARN without the `/*` suffix, since listing is an operation on the bucket resource itself, not on any individual object -- a second, separate statement with `"Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::reports-bucket"` would be needed for that, and it's a common follow-up bug to forget.

The `Action` array lists only `s3:GetObject` and `s3:PutObject` -- omitting `s3:DeleteObject` entirely satisfies 'never delete' more robustly than granting it and then trying to cancel it out with a separate Deny statement, since simply never allowing an action in the first place can't be defeated by a mismatched or missing Deny elsewhere. The `Resource` ARN, `arn:aws:s3:::user-uploads-bucket/uploads/*`, scopes access to only object keys that begin with the `uploads/` prefix inside that one bucket -- an object like `user-uploads-bucket/exports/report.csv` would not match this pattern at all. The policy deliberately does not include `s3:ListBucket`, since that's a bucket-level action (it would need the bare bucket ARN, `arn:aws:s3:::user-uploads-bucket`, as its Resource, not the object-level ARN used here) and the exercise only asked for get/put access to objects under a prefix -- least privilege means resisting the temptation to add 'while I'm at it' permissions that weren't actually requested.

# Under the hood, for every single object matching the old prefix, the CLI issues:
#   1. a CopyObject call to the new key
#   2. a DeleteObject call on the old key
# There is no single S3 API call that renames a prefix as one atomic operation.

# pseudocode for the current nightly job
for key in list_all_objects_under_prefix("data/2026-01-14/"):
    copy_object(from=key, to=key.replace("data/2026-01-14/", "archive/2026-01-14/"))
    delete_object(key)
# runs once per object, sequentially, for several million objects
expl: The fundamental issue is that this job is making two full API calls (one copy, one delete) per object, sequentially, for several million objects -- there is no way to make that fast as a strictly sequential loop, because S3 simply has no bulk-rename primitive to fall back on; the per-object cost the naive loop pays is real, not an artifact of writing the loop poorly. The most scalable fix is S3 Batch Operations, a managed feature specifically built for exactly this class of problem: given a manifest of object keys, it performs a specified operation (like copy) across all of them with built-in parallelism, automatic retries on transient failures, and progress tracking, without the calling application needing to manage a slow sequential loop itself. An even better fix, when it's an option, is avoiding the need for a bulk move altogether -- for instance, writing new data directly under the eventual archive-style key structure from the start, so 'reorganizing' never has to touch millions of pre-existing objects at all. The core lesson is that any design assuming S3 prefixes can be cheaply restructured after the fact is fighting the object-store model rather than working with it.

expl: The key fact driving this whole scenario is that `restore-db-instance-to-point-in-time` always creates a brand-new RDS instance rather than modifying the source instance in place -- so the instant the restore command finishes, there are simply two databases: the original `catalog-db`, unchanged and still serving traffic with the corrupted pricing data intact, and the new `catalog-db-restored`, containing a faithful snapshot of everything as of 08:59 UTC. Nothing about running the restore command automatically redirects any traffic, which is precisely why real users are still seeing the corrupted state immediately afterward -- the restore produced a correct *copy* of the data, not a live fix. The 46-minute gap between 08:59 and 09:45 also matters: any legitimate order or inventory change made on `catalog-db` during that window exists there but not on `catalog-db-restored`, so a full cutover without reconciling that gap would silently lose real, valid data alongside discarding the corruption -- which is exactly why 'restore and immediately redirect everything' is rarely the complete fix; verifying the restored data and reconciling the gap window are real, necessary manual steps, not a formality.

table: UsageEvents
partition_key: tenantTier   # "free" | "pro" | "enterprise"
symptom: "enterprise-tier writes throttled heavily; table-wide capacity metrics look healthy"
context: "one very large enterprise customer accounts for most of all events system-wide"
expl: `tenantTier` only ever has three possible values in this table, so every single item -- across every tenant that happens to share a tier -- hashes to one of only three physical partitions, and one giant enterprise customer's traffic is entirely confined to whichever single partition `"enterprise"` hashes to, no matter how much total capacity the table has been provisioned with overall. That's a textbook hot partition: the throttling is real and specific to that one partition's own throughput ceiling, even while table-wide metrics (which aggregate across all partitions, including the much lighter `"free"` and `"pro"` traffic) look healthy. Switching the partition key to `tenantId` gives every distinct tenant, including the large enterprise one, its own dedicated partition-key value, so traffic is distributed by actual tenant rather than collapsed onto three tier buckets -- the dominant enterprise tenant still generates a lot of traffic, but it's now isolated to its own partition rather than sharing one partition's throughput ceiling with every other enterprise-tier tenant combined. If 'all enterprise-tier events across every tenant' is still a genuinely needed query, that access pattern would now go through a secondary index on the `tenantTier` attribute rather than through the primary key, since the primary key's job has shifted to optimizing for the far more common per-tenant access pattern.

The sort key, `sentAt#messageId`, puts an ISO-8601 timestamp at the front specifically so that items under the same `roomId` are physically stored in chronological order, which is exactly what 'ordered from oldest to newest' requires with no extra sorting step, and it makes a date-range restriction a direct `BETWEEN` condition on the sort key rather than something requiring a filter pass over unrelated items. The `messageId` suffix exists purely to guarantee uniqueness in case two messages in the same room land on the identical timestamp, which a pure timestamp sort key alone couldn't guarantee. This schema satisfies the one stated access pattern with a single, efficient `Query` -- because that access pattern was designed into the key structure from the start, exactly the DynamoDB modeling discipline the explanation described, rather than being bolted on afterward with a scan or a secondary index.

Original reasoning: "DynamoDB is what modern, scalable teams use, so we built our
 new internal admin tool's data model on it."

Actual workload: a handful of internal staff, low request volume, and every
 week someone needs a genuinely new report -- filtered and grouped in ways
 nobody anticipated when the table was designed.

Symptom: every new report request means either a new secondary index (a
 real, recurring engineering task) or an accepted expensive Scan, for a
 workload with low overall traffic that never actually needed DynamoDB's
 scaling properties in the first place.

Corrected reasoning: low request volume + constantly evolving, unpredictable
 query needs -> RDS's query flexibility is the better fit; DynamoDB's
 scaling strength was never the actual bottleneck this workload had.

expl: Each answer follows directly from asking what the workload's actual access pattern is, rather than from any property of the service names themselves. Workload 1's unit of access is an entire file with no need for field-level querying, which is squarely S3's strength and would be an awkward fit for either RDS (which would need to store large blobs inside a relational row, generally discouraged) or DynamoDB (which has a per-item size limit far smaller than a typical video file). Workload 2's two operations are exactly the kind of small, fixed, extremely high-volume access pattern DynamoDB is designed around -- a top-100 leaderboard read and a per-player score update both map cleanly onto a well-chosen partition/sort key design, and DynamoDB's flat latency profile as the leaderboard grows is exactly the property this workload needs at that request volume. Workload 3's defining trait -- genuinely new, unanticipated query shapes every week -- is the one profile DynamoDB structurally struggles with, since each new query shape either needs a new access pattern designed into the table ahead of time or falls back to an expensive Scan; RDS's query planner and indexing handle this kind of variability as a matter of course, which is exactly the flexibility this workload actually needs.

  reason: "The unit of access is the whole video file itself, retrieved by key at large scale and low per-GB cost -- there's no need to query individual fields within the file."

workload_2: DynamoDB
  reason: "Both access patterns are fixed, simple, and known in advance, at very high volume -- exactly the profile DynamoDB's partition-key model scales for with flat, predictable latency regardless of leaderboard size."

workload_3: RDS
  reason: "Query needs are ad-hoc and change weekly in ways not known in advance -- exactly the varied, evolving access pattern a relational query planner and indexing are built to handle, versus DynamoDB, which would require a new access pattern (and likely a new index or Scan) for every new report shape."

  workloads:

The 'simplicity' of one store was illusory specifically for this one workload -- it wasn't actually simpler once the recurring Scan/index churn is counted as real, ongoing cost. The corrected design keeps DynamoDB exactly where it was already working well (catalog and orders) and moves the reporting workload to RDS, where ad-hoc, evolving queries are a core strength rather than a recurring fight against the store's design. A common way to keep both stores in sync is streaming changes from DynamoDB (via DynamoDB Streams) into the RDS-based reporting store, accepting some eventual-consistency lag for reporting purposes in exchange for reporting queries that no longer require redesigning the primary transactional table every time a manager asks a new question.

exp: Someone changed the RDS instance's automated backup retention from 7 days (what the template specifies) down to 0 (disabled) directly outside of CloudFormation -- likely to work around some issue during an incident, such as backup-related I/O contention. Left unaddressed, this means the database currently has no automated backups at all, a serious data-loss risk that isn't visible unless someone specifically runs drift detection, since the live database otherwise appears to be working fine.
expl: The drift result isolates exactly one property difference: `BackupRetentionPeriod` is `7` in the template but `0` on the live resource, meaning automated backups have been disabled on the actual database even though the template -- the presumed source of truth -- still says they should be running with a 7-day retention window. This is a specific, serious instance of the general drift risk: unlike a cosmetic setting, a disabled backup silently removes a safety net that nobody would necessarily notice is missing until the moment a backup is actually needed and isn't there. The fix requires a human decision, not just an automated one: either this change was a deliberate, temporary workaround that should be reverted immediately by redeploying the template (restoring backups), or there's a real reason backups needed to be disabled, in which case the template itself should be updated to reflect that decision explicitly and reviewably, rather than leaving the live database quietly diverged from what anyone reading the template would assume is true.

The safe response is to add `DeletionPolicy: Snapshot` (and typically `UpdateReplacePolicy: Snapshot` as well, which specifically governs the replacement-during-update case) before executing, ensuring a final snapshot is taken and preserved even though the instance itself is being replaced -- or, if snapshotting and restoring from it afterward isn't acceptable operationally, treating this as a signal to find a different approach to the storage-type change entirely, such as a manual, carefully-sequenced migration outside of a change that CloudFormation itself flags as requiring recreation.

exp: Whichever cdk deploy actually issues its update-stack call first (say, Engineer A's) transitions the stack into UPDATE_IN_PROGRESS. Engineer B's nearly-simultaneous update-stack call against the same stack is rejected by CloudFormation, since a stack only supports one update lifecycle at a time -- Engineer B's deploy fails outright rather than racing or corrupting anything. A pipeline avoids this scenario entirely (rather than just handling it safely after the fact) because a single merge queue feeding a single deploy stage means only one apply against a given environment is ever triggered at a time in the first place -- there's no possibility of two applies being kicked off concurrently to begin with.

expl: CloudFormation's own stack-level protection means this specific race doesn't corrupt anything -- only one update can be in progress against a given stack at a time, and a second concurrent attempt is simply rejected, with the rejected engineer needing to retry once the first update completes. This is a real safety net, but it's a reactive one: it prevents damage from the race, but the race (and the wasted attempt, the confusing rejected-command error, and the need to figure out who should retry and when) still happens. A pipeline with a single merge queue removes the race's precondition entirely, rather than just handling its consequences safely -- because merges (and the deploys they trigger) are processed one at a time through a single queue, there's structurally no way for two applies against the same environment to be triggered concurrently in the first place, which is a stronger guarantee than 'concurrent applies are handled safely if they happen.'

An instance in subnet-A, if it also has a public IP assigned, can be reached directly from the internet. An instance in subnet-B can never be reached by a connection initiated from the internet, but can still reach out to the internet (e.g. for updates or external API calls) via the NAT Gateway sitting in subnet-A.

expl: The determining factor for both subnets is exactly where their 0.0.0.0/0 route points, since that's what public/private actually means for a subnet. subnet-A's default route goes to an Internet Gateway, which is bidirectional -- it can both send an instance's outbound traffic to the internet and deliver inbound connections initiated from the internet, provided the target instance has a public (or Elastic) IP address. subnet-B's default route instead goes to a NAT Gateway, which fundamentally only works in one direction: it relays traffic that originated from inside the VPC out to the internet and routes the corresponding replies back, but it has no mechanism to accept a brand-new inbound connection initiated from the internet side at all -- there's no listening service on the NAT Gateway for an external client to connect to. This is exactly why private subnets are considered safe from unsolicited inbound internet traffic while still being able to reach external resources when they need to.

expl: unhealthy_threshold=2 means the ALB needs to see two consecutive failing checks before flipping the target to unhealthy -- the first failure at t=20s isn't enough on its own, but the second consecutive failure at t=30s crosses the threshold, so removal happens exactly at t=30s, not at t=20s (too early, only one failure so far) or t=40s (too late -- the instance is already excluded from rotation by then, so the third failure at t=40s doesn't change anything, it's simply confirming what's already true). #   env-B: request_count -> 1, 2
#   env-C: request_count -> 1
# There is no invocation anywhere that reports "5" -- there is no shared 5 at all.

exp: Invocation 1 is a cold start (no warm environment existed after an hour of idleness). Invocation 2 is very likely also a cold start (or lands on a second, newly created environment) if it arrives while invocation 1's single environment is still occupied handling invocation 1 -- Lambda creates a second environment to serve it concurrently rather than queuing it behind the first. Of invocations 3, 4, and 5, at most one or two can reuse whichever environment(s) survived from the first burst (if they're still warm 30 minutes later, which is plausible but not guaranteed), and the rest require newly created environments -- so at least one, and quite possibly all three, are cold starts.

t=0:00:00   invocation 1 arrives
t=0:00:00.2 invocation 2 arrives (200ms later)

expl: The core rule is: a cold start occurs whenever an invocation needs an execution environment and no suitable warm one is currently idle and available. Invocation 1 has no prior environment at all, so it's unambiguously cold. Invocation 2 arrives only 200ms after invocation 1 -- if invocation 1 is still running (a very plausible timeframe for it still to be executing), that environment isn't free to take invocation 2, so Lambda spins up a second environment concurrently, which is also a cold start for that second environment specifically, even though the function itself already has one warm environment elsewhere. By the time invocations 3, 4, and 5 arrive, 30 minutes have passed with no traffic -- environments can be reclaimed after periods of inactivity, so it's entirely possible neither of the two earlier environments survived; even in the best case where one did survive, it can only serve one of the three simultaneous invocations, leaving at least two needing brand-new, cold environments. The general lesson: cold starts aren't simply a 'first request of the day' phenomenon -- they recur any time concurrency needs outpace the currently warm environment pool, including during otherwise sustained traffic.

The original code works under low traffic purely by coincidence: with requests spaced far apart, they almost always land on the same single warm environment, so incrementing its one copy of `processed_today` happens to behave like a real shared counter. Under real concurrent load, Lambda creates multiple execution environments to serve overlapping requests, and each one has its own independent process with its own independent `processed_today` starting from whatever that specific environment's own history happens to be -- there is no single number being incremented at all, so different requests correctly but confusingly report different, individually-too-low counts, none of which reflects the true total across every environment. The fix moves the counter into DynamoDB, using an atomic `ADD` update expression: every environment, regardless of which one handles a given request, increments the exact same item in the exact same table, so the count is genuinely shared and consistent no matter how many concurrent environments Lambda happens to be running behind the scenes.

expl: The original handler returns a plain dictionary of business data -- there's no `statusCode` and no `body` field, and even if there were, `body` must be a JSON string, not a nested object. API Gateway's proxy integration can only construct a real HTTP response from a return value that matches its expected shape; a return value that doesn't match it causes API Gateway to give up and return a 502 to the client, entirely independent of whether the Lambda function itself executed correctly, which is exactly why CloudWatch shows no error at all -- from Lambda's point of view, nothing went wrong. The fix wraps the same business data in the required shape: an explicit `statusCode`, a `body` produced by serializing the data to a JSON string, and (for clarity to the client) a `Content-Type` header.

Creating the API, the integration, and the route only configures API Gateway's own side of the connection -- it does not grant API Gateway any permission to actually invoke the target Lambda function, because that permission lives on the Lambda function's resource-based policy, a separate piece of configuration entirely. Without it, every request that reaches the route fails at the invoke step before the function's own code ever runs, which is exactly why CloudWatch shows no invocation at all, not even a failed one -- the failure happens one level upstream of the function itself. `aws lambda add-permission` adds a statement to that resource-based policy granting the `apigateway.amazonaws.com` service principal `lambda:InvokeFunction` rights, scoped via `--source-arn` to this specific API (and, in this pattern, this specific route), so that some other unrelated API in the account can't invoke this function simply because it also happens to be an API Gateway API.

Once duplicated, there is no mechanism keeping the two copies in sync; a fix applied to one is simply absent from the other until someone notices, which is exactly what happened here. The fix extracts `place_order_with_tax` as a single shared function containing the actual business rule, leaving each handler responsible only for the platform-specific work of pulling `order_id` and `amount` out of its own event shape (API Gateway's `pathParameters`/`body`, or SQS's `Records` array) and calling the shared function. Any future tax-rate fix now needs to happen in exactly one place, and both triggers automatically get the fix, because both are thin call-throughs to the same underlying logic rather than independent copies of it. This is the same 'isolate the platform-specific glue' pattern from earlier in this concept, applied here to a multi-trigger scenario rather than a portability-across-clouds scenario -- the same discipline pays off in both cases.
